claims.text: Existing analytical conductivity approaches for HfNbTaTiZr assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Atomistic or mesoscale simulation of defect formation will predict electrical conductivity more accurately than existing analytical approaches.
The predicted accuracy advantage will apply in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The simulated material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen introduces vacancies into the HfNbTaTiZr crystal lattice.
Oxygen introduces interstitial defects into the HfNbTaTiZr crystal lattice.
Lattice defects alter pathways for electron mobility.
Changes in electron mobility caused by defects alter the material's electrical conductivity.
The simulations will predict conductivity variations that significantly deviate from existing analytical-model predictions.
Conductivity will increase at higher temperatures because defects become activated.
The hypothesis is limited to HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen and to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The magnitude of the conductivity change depends on the types and concentrations of simulated defects.
Agreement between measured and simulated conductivity to within 10% across the temperature ranges would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts improved simulation accuracy, but the falsification rule says that close agreement between measurement and simulation—less than 10% deviation—would falsify it. Such agreement would ordinarily support, not falsify, the accuracy claim.

The predicted outcome concerns superiority over existing analytical models, whereas the falsification rule tests only absolute simulation error and does not require the simulation to outperform those models.
